items.prompt: Which file extension is used for standard TypeScript source files (without JSX)?

options.label: .tsc
.js.ts
.ts
.typ

rubric: TypeScript source files use .ts.
'.tsc' is the name of the compiler command, not a file extension.

items.prompt: Which command-line tool compiles TypeScript into JavaScript?

options.label: nodets
tsx-build
jsc
tsc

rubric: tsc is the TypeScript compiler.
The others are not the standard compiler tool.

items.prompt: Which syntax correctly annotates a variable `age` as a number?

options.label: let number age = 30;
let age: number = 30;
let age as number = 30;
let age<number> = 30;

rubric: TypeScript puts the type after a colon following the name.
Other forms borrow syntax from other languages.

items.prompt: Which keyword declares a named object shape in TypeScript that exists only at compile time?

options.label: record
class
struct
interface

rubric: interface describes a shape and is erased when compiled.
class produces runtime JavaScript, so it is not compile-time only.

items.prompt: Which file normally holds a TypeScript project's compiler configuration?

options.label: tsconfig.json
package-lock.json
typescript.config.txt
tsc.settings

rubric: tsconfig.json configures tsc.
package-lock.json records dependency versions, not compiler options.

items.prompt: Which of the following are built-in primitive types in TypeScript? Select all that apply.

options.label: integer
number
array
boolean

items.prompt: A teammate writes `function first<T>(items: T[]): T { return items[0]; }`. You are asked to name the part written as `<T>`.

options.label: A decorator applied to the function
An HTML tag inside the code
A type parameter of a generic function
A type assertion on the function's return value

rubric: <T> declares a generic type parameter.
A type assertion uses 'as' or angle brackets before a value, not after a function name.

items.prompt: What happens to type annotations like `: number` when TypeScript is compiled to JavaScript?

options.label: They are converted to JSDoc tags
They are removed from the output
They become runtime checks
They become comments with the same text

rubric: Types are erased at compile time.
Believing they become runtime checks confuses static and dynamic checking.

items.prompt: Given `let count: number = 5;`, what will the compiler do with the later line `count = "five";`?

options.label: Convert it to NaN
Widen to string | number
Throw an error at runtime
Report a type error

rubric: Assigning a string to a number variable is a compile-time error.
Variables are not widened automatically after annotation.

items.prompt: What does the type `string[]` describe?

options.label: An array whose elements are all strings
A tuple with exactly one string
A string containing array brackets
An array of any values converted to strings

rubric: string[] is an array of strings.
A tuple fixes length and positions; it is not string[].

items.prompt: What does the type `string | number` mean for a variable?

options.label: It can hold either a string or a number
It must hold both a string and a number
It can hold any type at all
It holds a string converted to a number

rubric: A union allows one of the listed types.
Confusing union with intersection suggests it must be both.

items.prompt: In an interface, what does `nickname?: string` mean?

options.label: The property may be omitted
The property is computed lazily
The property must be a nullable string
The property is read-only

rubric: The ? marks an optional property.
Optional is different from readonly or null.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe what TypeScript's static type checking does? Select all that apply.

options.label: It can flag calling a function with the wrong argument type before the code runs
It guarantees that values from an external API match their declared types at runtime
It can catch a misspelled property name on a typed object
It makes the compiled JavaScript run faster

rubric: Static checks find mismatches and typos at compile time.
Types are erased, so they neither validate external data at runtime nor speed up execution.

items.prompt: A developer sets `"strict": true` in tsconfig.json. A colleague asks what that changes. The project already compiles with no errors under the old settings.

options.label: It makes the compiled code throw on type mismatches at runtime
It turns on a group of stricter checks, so new errors may appear
It only changes how the compiler formats output, such as semicolons and quotes
It removes all type annotations and comments from the emitted JavaScript

rubric: strict enables several stricter compile-time checks, which may reveal new errors.
It does not add runtime checks or change formatting.

items.prompt: What happens when `tsc` checks `let x: number = "5";`?

options.label: It compiles cleanly and then throws a TypeError when the line runs
It reports a compile error because a string is not assignable to number
It silently converts the string to the number 5 during compilation
It compiles cleanly and x holds a string, with a warning at runtime

rubric: TypeScript checks assignability statically and rejects string-to-number assignment.
Distractors assume type annotations convert values or are enforced at runtime.

items.prompt: What happens to an `interface` declaration in the JavaScript that `tsc` emits?

options.label: It is converted into a class with the same name in the output
It is kept as a comment block that the runtime validates against
It becomes a frozen object that is checked when values are used
It is removed entirely because types exist only at compile time

rubric: Interfaces are erased during compilation and leave no runtime trace.
Distractors treat types as runtime constructs.

items.prompt: What does the type `string | number` describe?

options.label: A value that may be either a string or a number
A value that must be both a string and a number at once
A value that is a string now and converted to number later
A pair holding one string and one number in that order

rubric: A union type allows any one of its member types.
Distractors confuse union with intersection, conversion, or tuples.

items.prompt: In `function identity<T>(x: T): T { return x; }`, what is `T`?

options.label: A base class that every argument passed to the function must extend, checked when the call is compiled
A built-in alias that is simply another way of writing the type `any` inside generics
A placeholder type filled in per call, linking input and return types
A runtime variable that stores the name of the argument's type as a string

rubric: T is a type parameter inferred or supplied at each call, so the return type matches the argument type.
Distractors treat T as a runtime value, as any, or as a base class.

items.prompt: What does setting `"strict": true` in tsconfig.json do?

options.label: It makes the emitted code throw errors whenever a type mismatches
It only forbids use of the `var` keyword throughout the project
It enables a family of stricter checks such as strictNullChecks
It minifies the emitted JavaScript to make the output files smaller

rubric: strict turns on a group of stricter type-checking flags.
Distractors confuse it with minification, runtime enforcement, or a lint rule.

items.prompt: Which statements about TypeScript type annotations are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: They are required on every variable declaration
They are erased from the emitted JavaScript
They convert values to the annotated type at runtime
They power editor autocompletion for objects
They help the compiler catch misspelled property names

rubric: Annotations are compile-time only, aid error detection and tooling.
Wrong options assume runtime conversion or mandatory annotation despite type inference.

items.prompt: A developer defines `interface User { name?: string }` and writes `function len(u: User) { return u.name.length; }`. The compiler reports "Object is possibly 'undefined'" on `u.name`. Why does this error appear?

options.label: Interface fields are unknown outside the file unless the `User` interface is exported
The `?` makes the type `string | undefined`, so `.length` may hit undefined
Under strict mode, `.length` is available only on arrays, not on plain strings
An optional field has no value until a default is assigned in the interface body

rubric: The `?` makes the property type include undefined, so access needs a check under strictNullChecks.
Distractors blame exports, string features, or defaults, none of which apply.

items.prompt: Given `interface Point { x: number; y: number }`, which declaration compiles without error?

options.label: `const p: Point = { x: 1 };`
`const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };`
`const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 };`
`const p: Point = { x: 1, y: "2" };`

rubric: Only the object with exactly x and y as numbers matches Point.
Others miss a property, use a wrong type, or add an excess property in a literal.

items.prompt: Which signature correctly types a function `sum` that takes an array of numbers and returns their total?

options.label: `function sum(nums[]: number): number`
`function sum(nums: number[]): void`
`function sum(nums: number): number[]`
`function sum(nums: number[]): number`

rubric: Parameter is number[] and the return is number.
Distractors swap types, return void, or use invalid syntax.

items.prompt: Given `function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined { return arr[0]; }`, what is the inferred type of `r` in `const r = first(["a", "b"]);`?

options.label: `string | undefined`
`any[]`
`string`

rubric: T is inferred as string, so the result is string | undefined.
Distractors ignore the undefined part or leave T unresolved.

items.prompt: Inside `function f(v: string | number) { if (typeof v === "string") { /* A */ } else { /* B */ } }`, which call compiles at comment B?

options.label: `v.trim()`
`v.length`
`v.toUpperCase()`
`v.toFixed(2)`

rubric: In the else branch v is narrowed to number, so toFixed is valid.
Other options are string members and fail on number.

items.prompt: You want the compiler to report an error whenever a function parameter has no type and none can be inferred. Which tsconfig option do you set?

options.label: `"target": "ES5"`
`"allowJs": true`
`"noImplicitAny": true`
`"skipLibCheck": true`

rubric: noImplicitAny flags parameters that would silently become any.
Others control JS inclusion, declaration file checks, or output version.

items.prompt: Which declarations compile under strict mode? Select all that apply.

options.label: `let d: boolean = 0;`
`let b: number[] = [1, "2"];`
`let a: string[] = ["x", "y"];`
`let c: [string, number] = ["age", 30];`
`let e: "on" | "off" = "on";`

rubric: The string array, the tuple, and the literal union are all valid.
b mixes types in a number array and d assigns a number to boolean.

items.prompt: Under strictNullChecks, a developer has `function getLength(s: string | null): number { return s.length; }` and gets an error. The function must return a number and return 0 for null input without crashing. Which fix does that?

options.label: `return s !== null ? s!.length : undefined;`
`return s?.length;`
`return s ? s.length : 0;`
`return (s as string).length ?? 0;`

rubric: The null check narrows s and gives 0 for null, keeping the return type number.
`!` and `as` compile but crash on null; `?.` yields number | undefined and fails the return type.

items.prompt: Given `function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined { return xs[0]; }`, what type does the compiler infer for `first(["a", "b"])`?

options.label: `string`, since the array has elements
`string | undefined`
`T | undefined`, as T stays unresolved
`any`, since no annotation is given

rubric: T is inferred as string from the array argument, so the return type is string | undefined.
Distractors ignore the declared undefined or treat the type parameter as unresolved.

items.prompt: What is the type of `Keys` in `type Keys = keyof { id: number; name: string }`?

options.label: `string`
`"id" & "name"`
`number | string`
`"id" | "name"`

rubric: keyof produces a union of the property-name literal types.
Distractors confuse keys with value types, widen to string, or use an intersection.

items.prompt: With `strict` enabled, given `interface User { id: number; name?: string }` and `const u: User = { id: 1 };`, what does tsc report for `const n: number = u.name.length;`?

options.label: No error, because `u` was assigned an object without `name`
An error: `u.name` is possibly `undefined`
An error: property `name` is required in `User`
An error: `length` does not exist on type `string`

rubric: An optional property has type string | undefined, and assignment narrowing does not apply to a non-union declared type.
Distractors assume assignment narrows the type or misread what optional means.

items.prompt: Given `interface User { id: number; name: string }` and `function update(u: User, patch: Partial<User>) {}`, which call compiles?

options.label: `update(u, "name")`
`update(u, { name: "Ann" })`
`update(u, { name: 5, id: 1 })`
`update(u, { id: 2, age: 3 })`

rubric: Partial makes every property optional but keeps its type, so a partial object with a string name is valid.
Distractors use a wrong value type, an unknown property that fails excess property checks, or a non-object.

items.prompt: Given `function f(x: string | number) { if (typeof x === "string") { return x.toUpperCase(); } /* here */ }`, which expression is valid at `/* here */`?

options.label: `x.toUpperCase()`
`x.length`
`x.toFixed(2)`
`x.toString().toFixed(2)`

rubric: After the string branch returns, x is narrowed to number, so toFixed is available.
Distractors assume x is still the full union or call number methods on a string.

items.prompt: Given `const pt = { x: 1, y: 2 } as const;`, which statements compile without error? Select all that apply.

options.label: `const b: number = pt.y;`
`const c = pt.z;`
`const a: 1 = pt.x;`

rubric: as const gives readonly literal types, so pt.x is 1 and pt.y (type 2) is assignable to number.
Assigning to a readonly property or reading a missing property is an error.

items.prompt: A team keeps some files as `.js` while migrating to TypeScript. They want tsc to include those files in the build and report type errors found through JSDoc annotations and inference. They edit `tsconfig.json`.

options.label: Set `"declaration": true`, since it generates types for JavaScript
Set `"allowJs": true` and `"checkJs": true` in compilerOptions
Set only `"noImplicitAny": true`, since it makes tsc analyse JavaScript
Set only `"allowJs": true`, since it type-checks included JavaScript files

rubric: allowJs includes JS files and checkJs reports type errors in them; both are needed.
allowJs alone only compiles them; noImplicitAny and declaration do not enable JS checking.

items.prompt: `const ids = [1, 2, 3]; const found = ids.find(i => i > 1); found.toFixed();` fails under `strict`. What is the cause?

options.label: The callback lacks a return type annotation, so `found` is untyped
`ids` is inferred as `any[]`, so calling `toFixed` is unsafe
`toFixed` is not defined on `number` values from arrays
`find` returns `number | undefined`, and `found` may be undefined

rubric: find can return undefined when nothing matches, so strictNullChecks rejects the direct call.
Other options misdiagnose inference of the array or the callback.

items.prompt: `const o = { a: 1, b: 2 }; const p: { a: number } = o;` compiles, but `const q: { a: number } = { a: 1, b: 2 };` errors. Why?

options.label: Object literals cannot be assigned to narrower types directly
Excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals
Variables are typed `any` once declared with `const`
Structural typing is applied only to inline object literals

rubric: Extra properties are allowed by structural typing, but a fresh literal triggers an excess property check to catch typos.
Distractors invent rules about const or reverse how structural typing works.

items.prompt: Under `strict`, `const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 }; Object.keys(obj).forEach(k => console.log(obj[k]));` errors on `obj[k]`. What is the root cause?

options.label: The `forEach` callback parameter `k` is implicitly `any`, so indexing fails
`obj` is inferred as `readonly`, so computed indexing on it is disallowed
The keys `a` and `b` are numbers, so `k` must be numeric to index `obj`
`Object.keys` returns `string[]`, and `string` cannot index `obj`

rubric: Object.keys returns string[], and a plain string is not known to be a key of obj under noImplicitAny.
Distractors blame readonly inference, forEach, or numeric keys.

items.prompt: `type Shape = { kind: "c"; r: number } | { kind: "s"; side: number }`. A `switch (s.kind)` handles both cases. Which addition makes the compiler flag any variant added later without a case?

options.label: An `if` chain with no `else` branch after the cases
`default: return (s as any).area;` to read area anyway
`default: const _x: never = s; return _x;`
`default: return 0;` to cover unexpected values

rubric: After all variants are handled s is never, so a new variant makes the never assignment fail to compile.
The other options silence or bypass the check instead of enforcing exhaustiveness.

items.prompt: The code `const users = JSON.parse(text) as User[];` compiles, but the app crashes when the server returns a different shape. What best explains this?

options.label: `User` is erased at compile time, so `JSON.parse` cannot build the objects
Strict mode removes type assertions, so parsed data is never checked
`as User[]` converts each parsed item into a `User`, and that conversion fails
`JSON.parse` returns `any`, so `as` asserts a type with no runtime check

rubric: Type assertions are compile-time only; the parsed data is never validated.
Distractors assume assertions convert data at runtime, that erasure stops parsing from building objects, or that strict mode is what leaves parsed data unchecked.

items.prompt: Given `function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]`, which statements are true of `pick({ a: 1, b: "x" }, "b")`? Select all that apply.

options.label: `K` is inferred as the literal type `"b"`
`pick({ a: 1, b: "x" }, "c")` is a compile error
The result is typed `number | string`
`K` is inferred as `string`, so any string key is accepted at compile time

items.prompt: A project passes `tsc` cleanly, but production logs show "Cannot read properties of undefined" from code like `user.profile.name`, where `profile` is sometimes missing. A reviewer notes `"strict"` is absent from `tsconfig.json`. What most likely explains why the compiler did not flag it?

options.label: `target` is set too low, so optional fields are never checked by the compiler
`skipLibCheck` is on, so declared interfaces are ignored when checking property access
`noImplicitAny` is off, so every property is silently typed as `any` and unchecked
`strictNullChecks` is off, so `undefined` is assignable to every type

rubric: Without strictNullChecks, null and undefined belong to every type, so a possibly missing profile is not reported.
The other flags affect implicit any, emitted syntax, or library declaration checking, not null safety.

items.prompt: Given `interface Opts { color: string }` and `const o = { color: 'red', size: 2 };`, the line `const a: Opts = o;` compiles but `const b: Opts = { color: 'red', size: 2 };` errors. Why?

options.label: Excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals; `o` is a variable, so structural typing tolerates the extra property
The compiler reports `size` only when `noImplicitAny` is on, and `o` has an implicit type that suppresses the error message
`const o` is widened to `Opts` on declaration, so the extra property is discarded before the assignment is ever checked at all
Literals are compared to `Opts` by nominal identity, while variables are compared structurally using only their property names

rubric: Excess property checking is limited to fresh object literals; non-fresh values are compared structurally.
Distractors suggest widening to the interface or nominal typing, which TypeScript does not do.

items.prompt: `const m: Record<string, number[]> = {}; m['a'].push(1);` compiles but throws at runtime. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: `Record` types are inferred as `any` for keys that were never assigned, so the compiler skips the check on `push` for those lookups
`strictNullChecks` ignores array element access, so only direct property reads on plain objects are checked for undefined
`const` disables null checking on the variable, because the binding cannot be reassigned later in the same scope
The index signature types every string key as `number[]`, so `undefined` is left out unless `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is on

rubric: Index signatures claim all keys exist; `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds `undefined` to lookups.
Distractors invent special rules for Record, arrays or const.

items.prompt: `function first<T>(a: T[], b: T): T { return a[0] ?? b }` is called as `first([1, 2], 'x')` and errors on `'x'`. What explains this?

options.label: String literals are never inferred as type arguments, so the call needs an explicit `<string>` annotation to compile cleanly
`T` is inferred as `number | string`, but the return statement then fails because `a[0]` may be undefined at runtime
Generic parameters default to `unknown`, and a string cannot be assigned to `unknown` when it sits in an array context
Inference takes `number` from the array argument, and `'x'` is not assignable to that chosen candidate

rubric: With candidates number and string and no common supertype, inference settles on the first candidate and rejects the other.
Distractors misdescribe inference as unions, unknown defaults or literal exclusion.

items.prompt: In `let id: string | undefined = get(); if (id) { items.forEach(i => use(i, id.length)); } id = undefined;` the callback reports `id` as possibly undefined. Why?

options.label: Because `id` is reassigned later, narrowing does not carry into the callback, which could run after the change
Callbacks passed to `forEach` are checked against declared types, because the compiler cannot tell whether such a callback runs synchronously
Truthiness checks narrow out `null` but not `undefined`, so `id` still includes `undefined` inside the block as well as in the callback
The callback parameter `i` shadows the outer scope, which resets the inferred types of captured variables when the callback is checked

rubric: Narrowing of a reassigned `let` is not preserved in closures, since the value could change before the callback runs.
Distractors claim truthiness ignores undefined or that shadowing resets types.

items.prompt: Under `strictFunctionTypes`, `interface A { h(e: Event): void }` accepts `{ h: (e: MouseEvent) => void }`, but `interface B { h: (e: Event) => void }` rejects it. What explains the difference?

options.label: The flag checks only members declared with arrow-function types, and method declarations are treated as a separate kind of callable that is exempt from the check
Interfaces whose members are methods are compared by member name and arity, while interfaces with property members receive a full structural comparison
Method-style members are compared bivariantly as a deliberate exception, while property function types are checked contravariantly
`MouseEvent` counts as a supertype of `Event` when the member is declared as a method, because method declarations get looser subtype rules for parameters

rubric: Method shorthand stays bivariant under strictFunctionTypes; function-typed properties are contravariant.
Distractors invent name-only comparison or hoisting rules.

items.prompt: A service compiles cleanly under `strict`, yet crashes with `Cannot read properties of undefined` on `order.customer.name`, where `order: Order` comes from an API. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: `Order.customer` is declared required, but the backend omits it for guest checkouts
`const order = (await res.json()) as Order` asserts a shape that nothing validated at runtime
`Order` was declared with `interface` rather than `type`, so its fields are erased at runtime
`strict` mode disables `strictNullChecks` for properties of imported types
`res.json()` returns `any`, which flows into `Order` without any check

rubric: Types are not checked at runtime: assertions, `any` leaks and inaccurate declarations all let bad data through.
Interface vs type and strict disabling nulls are not real causes.

items.prompt: A developer writes `const config = { mode: 'dark' }; setMode(config.mode);` where `function setMode(m: 'dark' | 'light')`. The compiler says `string` is not assignable to the parameter type. The developer is surprised because `config` is `const`. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.label: `setMode` is contravariant in its parameter, so the compiler requires `config.mode` to be a supertype such as `string | number`
`const` makes `config` read-only only at runtime, while the compiler still treats its properties as `any` until annotated
Object literals are always inferred as `Record<string, string>`, so `config.mode` becomes an index-signature lookup and loses its key
`const` fixes the binding, not the properties, so `mode` widens to `string`; keep the literal with `as const` or an annotation

rubric: Mutable properties of a literal widen to string; `as const` or a type annotation preserves the literal type.
Distractors confuse const with deep immutability or misapply variance.

items.prompt: A team models order status (`'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped'`). Criteria: values travel unchanged in JSON, no extra runtime code ships in the bundle, and invalid strings are rejected at compile time. Which is best?

options.label: A string-literal union type, since it erases at compile time and its values are the JSON strings themselves
A plain `string` alias with a doc comment, since the JSON payload is untyped anyway and extra checks add little value
A numeric `enum Status`, since members compile to compact numbers and the compiler rejects values that are not listed
A class with a private constructor and static instances, since it validates values at both runtime and compile time

rubric: A literal union meets all three criteria: no emitted code, JSON-identical values, compile-time rejection.
Numeric enums change the JSON values; classes add runtime code; a bare string accepts anything.

items.prompt: A plugin library exposes a `Config` shape. Criteria: downstream plugins must add their own typed fields from separate files, without editing the library source. Which declaration best meets this?

options.label: `interface Config { ... }`, because same-named interface declarations merge across files through module augmentation
`abstract class Config`, because subclasses in each plugin merge their added fields back into the base type
`type Config = { ... } & Record<string, unknown>`, because intersections let every plugin add typed fields automatically
`type Config = { ... }`, because aliases can be re-declared in module augmentations to add more fields

rubric: Only interfaces support declaration merging, which is what augmentation relies on.
Type aliases cannot be re-opened; intersections and subclasses do not alter the original type.

items.prompt: While migrating to `strict`, a team cannot fix 200 errors this sprint. Criteria: builds stay green, and suppressions that later become unnecessary must be noticed by the compiler. Which approach is best?

options.label: `as any` casts on affected expressions, since they are local and the compiler flags casts that become redundant
Turn `strict` off for the folder in tsconfig, since the setting re-enables itself once errors fall to zero
`// @ts-expect-error` with a TODO on each line, since the compiler errors once the line stops failing
`// @ts-ignore` on each line, since it silences errors now and the compiler warns when they disappear

rubric: `@ts-expect-error` itself becomes an error when no error remains, so stale suppressions surface.
`@ts-ignore` and `as any` stay silent forever; tsconfig flags never re-enable themselves.

items.prompt: `function isUser(x: unknown): x is User { return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null }` is used to validate API data. Judged against the criterion that a guard must never claim more than it checked, what is the verdict?

options.label: Sound: `typeof` narrowing to `object` is equivalent to checking `User`, because every interface describes an object value
Sound: the `unknown` parameter makes the compiler re-verify each `User` field at every call site that uses the guard
Unsound: it checks only for a non-null object, yet the predicate makes the compiler trust every `User` field
Unsound only because `x is User` requires a class, so `instanceof` is the only valid way to check a shape

rubric: The compiler trusts a type predicate without checking its body, so an under-checking guard creates false safety.
Distractors assume the compiler verifies guard bodies or that predicates need classes.

items.prompt: Criteria: `merge(a, b)` must accept objects of different shapes, and the result type must expose properties of both. Which signature is best?

options.label: `function merge<T>(a: T, b: Partial<T>): T`
`function merge<T extends object>(a: T, b: T): T`
`function merge(a: object, b: object): object`
`function merge<A extends object, B extends object>(a: A, b: B): A & B`

rubric: Two type parameters capture both shapes, and the intersection exposes both sets of properties.
A single T forces matching shapes; `object` loses properties; Partial<T> restricts b to T's keys.

items.prompt: A library's `getItems()` returns internal state. Criteria: callers must not mutate it through the types, and callers holding a `readonly Item[]` must be able to pass it to `summarise()`. Which changes meet the criteria? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keep `getItems(): Item[]` and add a doc comment forbidding mutation
Declare `summarise(items: readonly Item[])`
Declare `summarise(items: Item[])` so only mutable arrays are accepted
Declare `getItems(): readonly Item[]`

rubric: A readonly return type blocks mutation; a readonly parameter accepts both readonly and mutable arrays.
A doc comment is not enforced; a mutable parameter rejects readonly arrays.

items.prompt: A 300k-line JavaScript app ships weekly. Leadership wants strict type safety within a year without freezing feature work. Criteria: no big-bang rewrite, new code held to the strictest standard, progress measurable. Which plan is best?

options.label: Enable `strict` globally and silence each resulting error with `any`, so the whole codebase counts as typed from day one
Enable `allowJs`, convert files gradually, enforce `strict` on converted and new files, and track remaining JS files
Stay in JavaScript and add JSDoc comments with `checkJs` turned on at a lenient setting, then review the type coverage later
Rename all files to `.ts` in one long-lived branch with `strict: false`, then raise strictness after that branch finally merges

rubric: Incremental conversion with strict enforcement on new and converted files meets all three criteria.
Distractors are big-bang, unenforced, or hollow strictness through `any`.

items.prompt: An app reads `JSON.parse` output from an API whose shape changes occasionally. Criteria: bad payloads must be caught at runtime, and the field list must not be duplicated across type and check. Which approach is best?

options.label: Keep an interface plus a hand-written checker for each endpoint, kept in sync by code review and team convention alone
Write an interface and cast the parsed value with `as User`, since the compiler then verifies every field at runtime as well as at compile time
Validate with a runtime schema and derive the static type from that schema, so one definition drives both checking and typing
Type the parsed result as `any` and rely on strict mode to flag any mismatched field later when the code uses that value

rubric: A schema gives runtime validation and a single source of truth for the type.
Casts and `any` are erased and check nothing at runtime; duplicated checkers drift apart.

items.prompt: With `useUnknownInCatchVariables` on, a team debates how to read the message in `catch (e)`. Criteria: no unsafe property access, since any value can be thrown, and minimal ceremony. Which option is best?

options.label: Narrow with `e instanceof Error` before reading `message`, because thrown values can be strings or arbitrary objects
Turn the flag off project-wide so `e` is `any`, because narrowing every catch block costs more than it prevents
Cast with `e as Error` so the compiler adds a runtime check, because assertions verify the actual class of the value
Annotate `catch (e: any)` so `e.message` always compiles, because JavaScript guarantees every thrown value is an Error

rubric: Narrowing handles the fact that any value can be thrown, with a one-line check.
`any` and `as` skip verification; they assume what the language does not guarantee.

items.prompt: A lead claims: 'With `strict: true` and no explicit `any` in our code, runtime type errors in production are impossible.' Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: The compiler inserts runtime checks only for annotated parameters, so unannotated locals are where errors arise
The claim holds only while `skipLibCheck` is off, because library types are then verified when the code runs
`strict` leaves out `noImplicitAny`, so inferred `any` values slip through and cause runtime errors in typed code
Types are erased at compile time, so network, storage or untyped-library data can still violate declared types at runtime

rubric: Static types are erased; boundaries with external data remain unchecked.
`strict` does include `noImplicitAny`, and the compiler never inserts runtime type checks.

items.prompt: You maintain a library whose exported `Config` object shape must be extendable by plugin packages adding their own fields, with no change to library source. Which declaration is the best fit?

options.label: An `interface`, because only interfaces can appear in generic constraints such as `T extends Config` in signatures
A `type` alias, because aliases with the same name merge across declarations and combine their members automatically
An `interface`, because it can be reopened through declaration merging in other packages
A `type` alias, because interfaces cannot describe object shapes that include methods or optional members

rubric: Interfaces support declaration merging and module augmentation, which is what plugins need.
Type aliases cannot be redeclared, and both forms can describe methods and be used as constraints.

items.prompt: A codebase will be compiled by a per-file transpiler that strips types without cross-file analysis. Criteria: no extra emitted runtime code, exhaustive-check support, and safety under isolated per-file compilation. Which representation of a status set is best?

options.label: A `const enum`, because its values are always inlined correctly even when files are transpiled one at a time
A numeric `enum`, because reverse mapping lets the compiler verify exhaustiveness without any emitted lookup object
A regular `enum`, because it erases completely and keeps exhaustive checks without generating any runtime object
A union of string literals, because it erases fully and still supports exhaustive checks in every compilation mode

rubric: String literal unions emit nothing and work with per-file transpilation and `never` checks.
Enums emit objects, and `const enum` inlining is unreliable under isolated per-file compilation.

items.prompt: Under `strict`, TypeScript still has deliberate unsoundness. Which statements correctly identify real gaps a reviewer should weigh? Select all that apply.

options.label: Method parameters are checked bivariantly, so a handler accepting a narrower type can still be assigned
Arrays are covariant, so a `Dog[]` can be passed where `Animal[]` is expected and then mutated
Indexing `arr[i]` yields `T` rather than `T | undefined` unless `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is enabled
With `strict` on, `null` can still flow into any variable whose annotation excludes `null` and `undefined`
Assertions from `unknown` to a specific type are verified at runtime by the code the compiler emits

rubric: Method bivariance, array covariance and unchecked indexing are documented unsound areas.
Assertions emit no checks, and `strictNullChecks` does block null for non-nullable types.

items.prompt: A monorepo has 40 packages under one `tsconfig.json`, and CI type-checking takes 9 minutes although most PRs touch a single package. The team must keep full type checking and `.d.ts` output. Which change best meets these criteria?

options.label: Split into per-package projects using `composite` and `references`, then build with `tsc -b` so unchanged packages are skipped
Disable `strict` for all packages so the compiler performs fewer checks per file and finishes each run sooner
Switch CI to a transpile-only loader so type errors stop blocking merges and builds finish faster for every PR
Set `skipLibCheck` and `noEmit` everywhere so checking is faster, accepting that declaration files are no longer produced

rubric: Project references with `tsc -b` give incremental builds while keeping checking and declarations.
The other options drop type errors, strictness or declaration output, violating the stated constraints.

items.prompt: You need a utility type making an object and every nested object and array property readonly at all depths, with no manual per-type work. Which definition meets this?

options.label: `type DeepReadonly<T> = Readonly<Partial<T>>` which marks every property and nested property as readonly recursively
`type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }` applied once, since `readonly` propagates into all nested members
`type DeepReadonly<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }` which recurses but strips readonly at each level
`type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }` which recurses into every nested property

rubric: A recursive homomorphic mapped type with `readonly` applies at every level, including arrays.
Non-recursive versions are shallow, and `-readonly` removes the modifier.

items.prompt: Design the `on` method of a typed emitter for `interface Events { login: { id: string }; logout: void }`. Requirements: the handler payload type must follow the event name, and unknown names must fail to compile.

options.label: `on<K extends keyof Events>(name: K, handler: (payload: Events[K]) => void): void`
`on(name: string, handler: (payload: any) => void): void` since the string name selects the right payload at runtime
`on<T>(name: string, handler: (payload: T) => void): void` so each caller supplies the payload type it expects
`on(name: keyof Events, handler: (payload: Events[keyof Events]) => void): void` giving a single union payload type

rubric: A generic key linked to `Events[K]` ties payload to name and rejects unknown names.
Other signatures leave payload unlinked, untyped or a union that forces narrowing.

items.prompt: Create an ID type so a `UserId` cannot be passed where an `OrderId` is expected, with zero runtime overhead and values still being plain strings. Which design satisfies every constraint?

options.label: `enum UserId { }` and `enum OrderId { }` used as containers, since enums create distinct types without emitting any runtime code
`type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }`, with a helper that casts a string once at the boundary
`class UserId { constructor(readonly value: string) {} }` wrapping each ID, which keeps IDs distinct in the type system
`type UserId = string` and `type OrderId = string`, since distinct alias names make the compiler treat them as different

rubric: A branded intersection is distinct at compile time and erased at runtime.
Aliases are interchangeable, enums emit code, and classes add runtime wrappers.

items.prompt: A function handles `type Shape = Circle | Square | Triangle`, each with a literal `kind`. Design the `switch` ending so adding a fourth variant later produces a compile error at that function, not a silent runtime gap.

options.label: `default: return 0;` which returns a safe fallback value for any unrecognised shape variant at runtime
`default: break;` followed by a trailing comment listing which variants must be added when new ones appear
`default: { const unreachable: never = shape; throw new Error(String(unreachable)); }` after all cases
`default: console.warn('unknown shape');` so any new variant is reported in logs whenever it first appears

rubric: Assigning the remaining value to `never` fails compilation when a variant is unhandled.
Fallback, break or logging defaults compile fine and hide the missing case until runtime.

items.prompt: A library is bundled to JavaScript by esbuild, which does no type checking or declaration output. Design the `tsc` config role so consumers get accurate `.d.ts` files and the source is strictly checked.

options.label: `{ "strict": false, "declaration": true, "emitDeclarationOnly": true }` to keep declaration generation fast and simple
`{ "strict": true, "noEmit": true }` since the bundler output already carries all information that consumers need
`{ "strict": true, "isolatedModules": true }` since that option writes declaration files alongside bundled output
`{ "strict": true, "declaration": true, "emitDeclarationOnly": true }` with the bundler producing the JavaScript

rubric: Strict checking plus declaration-only emit complements a bundler that emits JS.
`noEmit` produces no `.d.ts`, relaxing strict weakens checks, and `isolatedModules` does not emit declarations.

items.prompt: Starting from a tsconfig with no strictness flags, you must make `arr[i]` typed as possibly `undefined` and reject explicitly assigning `undefined` to an optional property `x?: number`. Which flags must you enable? Select all that apply.

options.label: `esModuleInterop`, which tightens how indexed and optional values are typed
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, which forbids explicit `undefined` on an optional property
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, which adds `undefined` to results of index access
`strictNullChecks`, which makes `undefined` a distinct type the other two flags rely on
`skipLibCheck`, which makes the compiler check optional properties more strictly

rubric: The two targeted flags need `strictNullChecks` so that `undefined` is tracked as its own type.
`skipLibCheck` and `esModuleInterop` are unrelated to indexing or optional properties.

items.prompt: You are writing a `fetchJson` helper used at 30 call sites. Requirements: callers get a precise return type, `res.json()` is never cast unchecked, and a malformed payload fails at the boundary with a clear error. Which design meets all three?

options.label: `fetchJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T>` that returns `res.json() as Promise<T>`, with each caller supplying the expected `T`
`fetchJson(url: string): Promise<unknown>` and every one of the 30 callers narrows it with an `as` cast
`fetchJson(url: string): Promise<any>` so callers annotate their own variables with whatever type they need afterwards
`fetchJson<T>(url: string, guard: (x: unknown) => x is T): Promise<T>` that throws when the guard rejects the body

rubric: Passing a type-guard lets the helper validate at runtime and return a precisely typed value.
Casts and `any` perform no validation, so bad payloads would flow into the program.
